sources.text:
Remember when the UAE told Bush a week before 9/11 that Al Qaeda was about to launch a major terrorist attack and Bush didn’t even tell the NSA?
Well that didn’t actually happen, but this right here seems to have:
Benjamin Netanyahu was personally alerted by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a large-scale offensive against Israel a week before its 7 October 2023 attack, but did not act on the warning, according to a book by Haaretz reporters.
The claim, which comes amid a crucial election campaign, prompted Israeli opposition leaders to describe the prime minister as “unfit” for office, even as Netanyahu denounced the report as an “absolute lie” and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.
Haaretz said the Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the militants were preparing “a terrifying operation” which he described as an “earthquake”.
According to the report, the UAE president, Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, spoke to Netanyahu a week and a half before the attack, and told him Hamas was planning a major operation. . . .
The claims are contained in the book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, which, its authors say, is based on dozens of sources in Israel and worldwide, including very senior officials.
According to Haaretz, bin Zayed communicated frequently with senior Israeli leaders, including Netanyahu and the Israeli president Isaac Herzog, with a UAE diplomat delivering a secure phone to the Israeli prime minister for the conversations.
A week and a half before 7 October, the reporters say, bin Zayed called Netanyahu from the presidential palace in Abu Dhabi and, in a 45-minute call, warned that Sinwar was planning a major operation which the Emirati leader was concerned could destabilise the region.
To bin Zayed’s surprise, Netanyahu reacted calmly to the news, the report said.
In a joint statement on Tuesday, several Israeli opposition party leaders declared their intention to find out what Netanyahu knew and when, and what actions he took, if any.
“Why did he not inform the security establishment, and why did he not act to protect Israeli citizens?” the statement demanded.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former military commander who has emerged as Netanyahu’s main rival in the October elections, accused the long-serving prime minister of evading responsibility for security lapses and resorting to “pathetic” excuses, such as saying he was not woken up soon enough on the morning of the attack.
“Netanyahu received dozens of warnings for 7 October and ignored them all. He is unfit,” Eisenkot wrote on X.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister also running in the elections, said Netanyahu “bears personal and direct responsibility” for the deaths on 7 October, the deadliest attack in Israeli history. “Netanyahu cannot continue to serve in his position for even one more minute,” Bennett said.
The leader of the centre-left Democrats party, Yair Golan, accused Netanyahu of “endangering Israel”.
“The stories about ‘no one woke me up’ are over. You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame,” he said, in a video posted on social media.
Israel’s elections are seven weeks away.
At this point it’s completely plausible that Netanyahu wanted the attacks to happen, and to lead to the murder of many civilians, because those deaths would advance his political goals, and also help keep him out of jail.

More evidence has emerged showing that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had prior knowledge of the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, attack but did nothing to stop it, ultimately using the attack and the lives of the Israeli captives as justification to carry out genocide in Gaza.
A report published in Haaretz reveals that the president of the United Arab Emirates, Mohamed bin Zayed, had a 45-minute conversation with Netanyahu a week and a half before the October 7 attack, warning that Hamas was preparing for a “major event.” One of bin Zayed’s advisers, a Palestinian émigré from Gaza, said that bin Zayed “recommended trying to find an economic solution” to prevent any escalation from Hamas.
Bin Zayed also warned Joe Biden’s CIA director, William J. Burns, that “something there is about to explode,” the report says.
But Netanyahu was unfazed, sources said, replying that Israel was ready for anything, and that he believed that Hamas would be taking action in the occupied West Bank. He did not tell the Israeli intelligence agencies, Shin Bet or Mossad, or the Israeli military about bin Zayed’s message — something the Emirati leader never imagined.
Ultimately, Hamas did launch an attack on October 7, 2023, in which around 1,200 people were killed in Israel. That attack has since been invoked countless times as supposed justification for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
Ahead of highly contested elections in Israel next month, Netanyahu’s handling of the attack has recently been under particular scrutiny — including other reports that Netanyahu took hours to respond on the day of the attack, and that his government issued a directive allowing Israeli soldiers to kill their fellow troops in order to prevent hostage-taking that day.
The Emirati president’s warning to Netanyahu came after months of negotiations between a Hamas political official and an Israeli Shin Bet official, mediated by a Fatah official, with the hopes of striking an agreement for long-term stability for Gaza. Prior to October 7, Israel had been maintaining a blockade on Gaza that had already created a humanitarian crisis, with widespread poverty and hunger imposed on the Palestinian population.
During these negotiations, the parties discussed improving Gaza’s economic conditions and a prisoner exchange in which Hamas would release Israeli prisoners and soldiers held in the Strip and Israel would release a few dozen Palestinian prisoners. But even as the deal was being finalized, Netanyahu delayed taking the last steps to solidify it.
After the delays, Hamas’s leader, Yahya Sinwar, pulled away from negotiations, and told the Fatah official to communicate to Israel that he was preparing for war, the report claims. The message was relayed to Shin Bet, who also warned Netanyahu about Sinwar’s threat.
In the days after the attack, as Israel was launching its all-out assault on Gaza, Sinwar also offered to release all of the civilian captives being held in Gaza, with the remaining captives being held for talks to end Israel’s incursions into the Strip.
Israeli leaders demurred. They responded by saying that the only thing they were interested in was supposedly eliminating Hamas.
“To be honest,” a senior Israeli military official said, “the issue of the hostages was not seriously on the agenda at this stage, and no one at the military or political level was open to discussing the proposal. The release of the hostages did not even enter the list of war objectives formulated by the government on the night of October 7. Could the proposal have been properly discussed and a decision reached? In substantive terms, the answer is yes.”
Netanyahu’s office has called the report an “absolute lie.” In a statement, the office said that “No warning was given to the Prime Minister from the United Arab Emirates before October 7th.”
Previous reports, however, have also found that Netanyahu and the Israeli military were warned about October 7 multiple times ahead of the attack, but did little to nothing to prepare or prevent it.

sources.news_title: Making Sense of That Big Story Saying Netanyahu Was Warned About Oct 7
sources.text:
The Israeli daily Haaretz published a big and consequential exposé today alleging that weeks before the October 7, 2023 massacres in southern Israel the head of the UAE, Mohamed bin Zayed, warned Prime Minister Netanyahu in a direct phone call lasting some 45 minutes that something big was coming from Hamas. For additional context, Israel holds elections on October 27 of this year. And as it has for the last three years, Netanyahu’s degree of responsibility for what happened remains a central question in the election. So while it’s not explicitly noted in the article, the electoral implications are clear. The investigation itself appears to be essentially an excerpt from a soon-to-be released book. So it’s not precisely a Haaretz story, more one that they’re publishing, though that’s fine print. The article is long and detailed and I think quite credible. But it’s paywalled. So I wanted to walk you through the key details and provide some general analysis.
It’s best to think of this piece as three separate revelations. The first is that — all according to this article — Israel and Hamas in 2023 were pretty close to finalizing a semi-normalization of the situation in Gaza in a longterm truce, or “hudna,” between Hamas and Israel. The details of this aren’t fully sketched out but basically an end to the blockade, freer commerce and travel through Israel and Egypt, etc. Second is the warning from MBZ in the weeks before the attack. Then, finally, it claims that in the immediate aftermath of the attacks Hamas, was willing to free most or all of the hostages, probably excluding military-aged men in or out of uniform, with few if any conditions.
The axis of the story is the relationship between revelations one and two. And to avoid too many qualifying clauses in this description below I will be asserting the claims of the article except where I say otherwise.
The central player here is Yahya Sinwar, the late leader of Hamas in the Gaza Strip. When Sinwar came to power in 2017 he brought a new militancy to the position and embarked on a program of greatly expanding and intensifying Hamas’ military capacity, including its tunnel system. He wanted to go to war with Israel. But in this he was also acutely aware of the fact that every time the Palestinians or Hamas had done so in the past, the actions had been decisively crushed by Israeli military might and intelligence. So while preparing for war and confrontation, he decided to also explore a deal that could qualitatively improve life for Palestinians living in the Strip. Those negotiations were very far along at the end of the summer of 2023. They bogged down when Prime Minister Netanyahu started dragging his feet on just how many and which Palestinian prisoners would be released as part of the deal.
The background here is that, notwithstanding Benjamin Netanyahu’s reputation as a hawk and a war-monger on the left in the U.S., at least until 2023 his characteristic action was more kicking the can down the road. Biding his time, not committing himself. There were already a lot of clashes in the West Bank at the time and a major domestic political crisis in Israel over the “judicial coup,” which had brought the anti-Netanyahu opposition out on to the streets every week for almost a year. This all came after five successive elections which were indecisive and one of which took him out of power for a year before finally allowing him to create a narrow coalition relying heavily on the Israeli far right. So the general thrust of the article is some mix of Netanyahu having his hands full and doing his standard slow-rolling. He also probably wasn’t eager to agree to a deal that might put his coalition under strain.
Finally, Sinwar lost his patience with the process and cut off negotiations. This was in September. So like a month before the attacks. He must have had everything ready for an attack. But this would have been when he put the plan into motion. Intermediaries who had been working the Hudna negotiations got wind of something coming and Sinwar himself made a threat to one of these intermediaries and told him to get the message to Israel.
It’s a little hard to see the logic of this other than as an attempt to get Netanyahu back to the negotiations since the element of surprise was essential to the eventual attack’s success. Indeed, Sinwar seems to have said as much. Without the element of surprise it couldn’t work. So even these warnings were risky. The intermediary was uncertain and even afraid of what to do with the information, partly fearing that in conveying the message to Israel he might be held responsible for it. So he went to MBZ, the leader of the UAE. He was highly concerned about an attack that could lead to more or less what has happened over the last three years: a catastrophic attack on Israel, followed by horrific retaliation against Hamas in Gaza and leading to a regional war. He told the intermediary to get the message to the Israelis. He did that at the security and defense level. But the warnings were fairly vague and not much happened in response to the warnings. Netanyahu was briefed on the message and the meetings, as would be the norm.
A key backdrop to all of this is that Israel did not take Hamas seriously as a military threat. They took Hezbollah very seriously, as a de facto state/army. Hamas was different, basically a terrorist threat which could fire off homemade rockets and mount terrorist attacks, but not a true military threat. So I think it’s fair to say that when they heard Hamas was warning of something big they simply didn’t believe the scale they were later able to pull off. They apparently decided that Hamas would try to get possession of Israeli academic Elizabeth Tsurkov who had been kidnapped in Iraq and was being held hostage there. (She was eventually released in September 2025.) In any case, MBZ didn’t get the reaction he wanted. But he was also afraid that a more specific warning to the Israelis might prompt a massive preemptive attack on Hamas in Gaza. He wanted to know more. So he sent the intermediary back to find more details and to talk to Sinwar.
The intermediary talked again to Sinwar who gave a more direct and grave message. The intermediary and then MBZ got the message that some sort of catastrophic attack was planned. So MBZ made the decision to talk to Netanyahu directly. He conveyed all this in a 45 minute call between the two men. The kicker here is that Netanyahu did not brief any of his security or defense officials on this outreach. Of course they’d already gotten a version of the message. But the direct contact from a the leader of the UAE obviously showed a different level of urgency and gravity. The argument, and it’s a pretty good one, is that if Netanyahu had briefed the heads of Mossad, the Shin Bet and the IDF about this call they would have taken more aggressive protective measures.
To cite just one example, in the hours just before the October 7 attack, Israel saw something was happening in Gaza. Security officials met to evaluate it and they decided it was likely a drill and not to mobilize. Of course, it was not a drill. It was the beginning mobilization for the attack. These are all what ifs of course. But it does not seem implausible that if Netanyahu had briefed these officials on this warning that that conclusion arrived at in those overnight meetings might have been different and Israel could have had some level of military response in place when the attack started.
Finally, we have the possibility of a hostage release immediately after the attacks. Here this sounds quite plausible but I think this is an incomplete perspective and perhaps to an American audience misleading. Once the attack happened, all the regional leaders were desperately scrambling to stop what was coming. The government of Qatar threatened to expel Hamas from the country if they didn’t immediately release all the civilian hostages. (As I noted above, there’s some disagreement over the definitions of civilians: Hamas likely viewed all military age men and possibly everyone of military age as soldiers, whether currently in the IDF or not.) Hamas first agreed to release the civilian hostages with a number of conditions, essentially non-retaliation for the attacks and some changes to the status quo on the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif. This was a non-starter. Other players intervened and basically said no conditions. Just release them. Hamas then appears to have agreed to this, with perhaps some token conditions.
The response from Israel was there’s nothing to talk about. Then Mossad Director David Barnea told Prime Minister al-Thani of Qatar: “If they want to release the civilians, let them release them. We are not prepared to speak with Hamas.” The same message was passed through other channels.
The offer and the response are both extremely plausible. But I think it was basically inevitable. I’m not trying to litigate here what you or I or anyone else thinks makes sense or what would have been right. But at that moment about 1200 Israelis, the great majority civilians, had been killed. What was being proposed here was a release of most of the hostages and a return to some sort of negotiations. At that moment that was acceptable only to the tiniest fringe of Israeli public opinion. The verdict was that Israel had misjudged Hamas and fatally underestimated it and that the only solution was to destroy it as an organization and kill everyone who had been involved in the attack. So my point is I don’t think this revelation, if it is one, is a surprise. And I don’t think it’s either here or there in terms of it political ramifications within Israel. Because every other party and leader who is now at all contesting for power would have made the same decision.
The only slight caveat to that is that it became clear over time that Netanyahu’s government had no real interest or priority to seek the release of the hostages at all, even long after Israel had delivered that decisive and ferocious assault and killed tens of thousands of civilians along the way. Some of that lack of interest was the government’s hawkishness and desire for revenge. But it was also because at a basic level Netanyahu did not want to bring the war to a close because that would create perhaps-unstoppable pressure to hold new elections that he would almost certainly lose. (As it happens, he waited till the last possible legal date to hold a new election.) That fact may change some of the shading of this revelation. But I don’t think it changes that big picture.
And finally, does any of this matter for the upcoming election? I’m honestly not sure. I went around the Israeli papers and the story is getting reported though not necessarily with screaming headlines basically everywhere. By rights it should fundamentally discredit Netanyahu whose calling card has always been security and normalcy. But he’s already been discredited to anyone without an overwhelming personal or ideological commitment to supporting him. Whatever messages or warnings Netanyahu received in the weeks before October 7, the bigger story is that Netanyahu had been Prime Minister for the previous 14 years with only one short one year interruption in 2021 and 2022. All the policies, strategies and decisions were his — both in the moment and in the shaping of policy back to 2009. And it happened on his watch. Given that political context my best guess would be a moderate political hit if only because he’s already down to the hard core of the rightist camp. But I emphasize “guess.” I really don’t know.

sources.news_title: Did Netanyahu ignore an Oct. 7 warning? Voters will decide who gets to investigate
sources.text:
Did Netanyahu ignore an Oct. 7 warning? Voters will decide who gets to investigate
A devastating new investigation says Netanyahu was warned of Hamas’ attack before Oct. 7 by the president of the UAE, making the case for a state commission of inquiry stronger than ever.
Israel’s election campaign effectively begins today, as political parties submit their list of candidates who will contest the Oct. 27 election. It is difficult to imagine a more politically explosive moment for the publication of a new investigation into the failures surrounding Oct. 7.
Today’s report in the Haaretz newspaper alleges that Benjamin Netanyahu received an extraordinary personal warning from UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed roughly a week and a half before the Hamas attack. According to the report, bin Zayed told Netanyahu during a 45-minute telephone conversation that Hamas chief Yahya Sinwar was preparing a major operation against Israel that could cause bloodshed and destabilize the region.
Netanyahu reportedly replied that he believed Hamas was focused on the West Bank and assured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared. The Haaretz report cites multiple senior foreign sources reportedly briefed on the conversation and an adviser to bin Zayed who was present for the call.
Even more consequentially, the investigation says Netanyahu did not pass this specific warning to the heads of the Shin Bet, Mossad or Israel Defense Forces. Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief Herzi Halevi, for their part, told Haaretz that they had not been informed of such a warning, while the UAE president did not respond to the news organization.
Haaretz traces the warning to an earlier chain of intelligence in which Sinwar himself had spoken ominously of an approaching “earthquake” – an enormous operation. That warning reached the Shin Bet on September 15 and produced high-level discussions in which Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar warned that Israel was moving toward confrontation.
Veteran journalist Shlomi Eldar, the co-author of the report, said bin Zayed concluded Israel had not heeded such signals – but Netanyahu “tried to convince bin Zayed that we are fine with Gaza.”
Netanyahu denies the central allegation completely. “There was no such warning,” his spokesman Topaz Luk said on Israel Radio. “I think this is another effort to distort the truth ahead of elections.”
The question of who is telling the truth leads directly to a democratic mechanism that has repeatedly been called upon at moments of national trauma throughout Israel’s history: a commission of inquiry.
That very mechanism was employed in response to the catastrophic failures surrounding the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when the Agranat Commission investigated the conduct of the military and government. State commissions of inquiry have likewise examined the 1982 Sabra and Shatila massacre and the killing of Arab citizens by police in October 2000.
Oct. 7 was the greatest security failure in Israel’s history, leaving more than 1,000 people dead, hundreds taken hostage, communities overrun and the country plunged into years of war.
Netanyahu has resisted all calls to establish an independent state commission – trying instead to set up an inquiry in which the opposition and coalition politicians would have equal say, guaranteeing any findings would be politicized. He has also attempted to deflect all blame onto the security establishment – making the issue a central one in the election campaign.
“You knew, you ignored it, you failed and you are guilty,” said opposition politician Yair Golan Tuesday, addressing his comments to Netanyahu. “We will set up a state inquiry that will expose the truth and those guilty will have to face justice .. for negligence that caused a massacre.”
Under the Commissions of Inquiry Law adopted in 1968, once the government establishes a state commission, its members are appointed by the president of the Supreme Court, and its chairman must be a serving or retired judge. The arrangement is intended to give the investigation independence from the political figures and institutions whose decisions it may ultimately have to judge.
And therein lies a rather extraordinary convergence. Netanyahu and his government have spent years attacking the legitimacy of precisely the institution entrusted by law with ensuring the independence of such an investigation: the Supreme Court. The campaign to weaken the judiciary that tore Israel apart before Oct. 7 has since provided a convenient argument against using the established mechanism for investigating Oct. 7 itself.
Netanyahu argues that a commission whose members are selected by the Supreme Court president cannot command broad public confidence. His opponents argue that a bespoke “political commission” may sound superficially balanced, but conclusions associated with coalition appointees would inevitably be dismissed by Netanyahu’s opponents as an attempt to protect him. Meanwhile findings associated with opposition appointees would be portrayed by his supporters as an attempt to destroy him. Israel would begin with two political camps choosing investigators and almost certainly end with two political camps accepting different versions of the truth.
The opposition has therefore refused to participate, arguing that the proposal would allow Netanyahu to influence the investigation of his own government. The stalemate has produced an outcome that is increasingly difficult to view as accidental: there is no agreed commission, no authoritative account of what happened and an ever-expanding vacuum in which every faction is free to construct its own version of Oct. 7.
Into that vacuum has flowed something far more disturbing than an ordinary argument over political responsibility. Netanyahu has worked relentlessly to shift responsibility toward the intelligence chiefs, the generals and especially the Shin Bet. Around him has grown an increasingly elaborate conspiracy theory that Oct. 7 may have involved something more sinister than incompetence and catastrophic misjudgment: an internal betrayal designed to damage Netanyahu politically.
What the Haaretz report provides is another powerful indication of how much remains unresolved, along with a potentially devastating explanation for Netanyahu’s determination to keep the established investigative mechanism from examining it. If the report is substantially correct — if Netanyahu personally received another serious warning before Oct. 7, misunderstood its significance, failed to circulate it to the security chiefs and then spent years attempting to redirect responsibility toward those same institutions — his resistance to a genuinely independent inquiry is clearly a political calculation..
“It’s like a knife in the stomach,” said Merav Svirsky, whose parents were killed in Kibbutz Be’eri, one of the communities hardest hit on Oct. 7, and whose brother was kidnapped and killed in Gaza. “My father and mother could have been alive. My brother would not have been kidnapped and would be alive. And while others resigned, Netanyahu clings to his seat.”
As we welcome the new year, the shofar’s blast cuts through the noise to wake us up. It calls for truth and accountability within ourselves and for the world.
The Forward takes the call for truth and accountability seriously. Readers come to the Forward for Jewish news they can trust, free of barriers or bias. They want the American Jewish story to be told fully and fairly.
We rely on our readers to help us heed the shofar’s call. I’m counting on you to make a generous gift to the Forward during the High Holiday season and help us reach our goal of $180,000.
— Benyamin Cohen, Senior Writer

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Denies Pre-Oct. 7 UAE Warning; Rivals Seek Probe
sources.text:
Israel's four main opposition leaders issued a rare joint statement on Tuesday demanding "an immediate and thorough investigation" into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct before the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack, after the newspaper Haaretz reported that the president of the United Arab Emirates had personally warned him roughly 10 days beforehand that Hamas was preparing a major operation — and that he told no one in Israel's security establishment. The Prime Minister's Office called the report "a total lie" and said Netanyahu "did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and received no warning from him." With a general election less than two months away, the dispute has moved the question of what the prime minister knew from the domain of a future inquiry into the center of the campaign.
The Haaretz report is drawn from a forthcoming book, "Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment," by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, and rests on interviews with dozens of sources in Israel and abroad. Its central claim is that Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in a 45-minute telephone call at the end of September 2023, told Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning action that would cause bloodshed, destabilize the region and endanger the Abraham Accords, and that Netanyahu replied that Israel was on top of the situation in Gaza, that any Hamas move was more likely to come in the West Bank, and that Israel was prepared for every scenario. The paper says three senior foreign officials were briefed on the call afterward, and cites a Palestinian adviser to the Emirati president, present for the conversation, as its principal source. It also reports that MBZ shared his concern with CIA Director William Burns. The Emirati government has not commented. Ronen Bar and Herzi Halevi, then the heads of the Shin Bet and the military, told Haaretz they were never informed of any such warning.
The chain the book describes begins not in Abu Dhabi but in Gaza. According to the report, a Fatah intermediary who had spent 2023 shuttling messages between Sinwar's representative and a Shin Bet officer over a prisoner-for-hostages arrangement — a deal the paper says was close to completion by summer, with Netanyahu having approved the release of 30 prisoners — was told by Sinwar in two private meetings in September that if Israel did not move, he was preparing "a huge surprise," a zilzal, an earthquake. The intermediary, fearing both Sinwar and the Israelis, took the warning to the Emirati adviser rather than to the Shin Bet; MBZ, initially cautious, concluded after the second meeting that Hamas intended war and called Netanyahu himself. The report says the Fatah intermediary and the adviser did eventually pass the warning directly to the Shin Bet in mid-September, that Israeli officials deliberated and did not read it as a threat from Gaza, and that on Oct. 1 Bar again proposed pre-emptive action against Hamas leaders without the prime minister mentioning his conversation with the Emirati ruler. "If we had known about the warnings," a senior Shin Bet official is quoted as saying, "there's a chance it would have given much greater weight to the initial message that reached us from Sinwar."
That is the report. Its evidentiary weight is a matter the reader can assess: a single newspaper, a book not yet published, an unnamed adviser as principal witness, a categorical denial from the prime minister's office, no comment from the Emirati side, and two former security chiefs confirming only that they were not told — which is consistent with the report and also with the call never having happened. Haaretz notes a parallel: days after the attack, Ynet reported that Egypt's intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel, had warned Netanyahu 10 days beforehand of "something unusual, a terrible operation" from Gaza. Netanyahu denied that conversation too.
The political reaction did not wait for corroboration. Naftali Bennett, the former prime minister who now leads the B'Yachad party, wrote on X that the report "is true" and that Netanyahu "bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch," without saying how he knew. Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff whose Yashar party is Netanyahu's main challenger, wrote that "more and more signs point to the same conclusion: Netanyahu led Israel blindly into the October 7 disaster," and promised a state commission of inquiry "as soon as the next government is formed." Yair Golan of The Democrats, who rescued civilians on the morning of the attack, said the prime minister's "place is in prison." Avigdor Liberman joined them in the four-party statement, which asked: "What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn't update the security establishment, and why he didn't act to protect Israeli civilians?"
The timing cuts against the prime minister for a reason beyond the election calendar. Netanyahu's office last week published a minute-by-minute account of his morning on Oct. 7, in response to what it called inaccurate reporting, showing a first update at 6:29 a.m., a departure for military headquarters at 7:30 and orders for full mobilization and a sealed border — placed, in the office's own timeline, at 9:55. Earlier this week he went further, criticizing the security chiefs for not waking him in the hours before the attack when, he said, "all the signs were there," and asserting that had they done so the attack "would not have taken place." Channel 12 reported Friday that he took at least two hours to leave his Caesarea home and did not contact the heads of the IDF or Shin Bet in that time. The Haaretz report, whatever its ultimate standing, lands on an argument the prime minister himself chose to open: that the failure was one of information not reaching him. A warning delivered to him personally, and not passed on, would invert that argument, which is why the opposition seized on it and why the denial was unqualified.
Netanyahu is, by now, the last senior official from that morning still in office. The defense minister, the chief of staff, and the heads of military intelligence, the Mossad and the Shin Bet have all resigned, been removed or reached the end of their terms; several have said publicly that they bear responsibility. Netanyahu has said he will answer for his part "later," has resisted a state commission of inquiry with the powers to compel testimony, and has proposed instead a government-appointed body the opposition calls a whitewash. The election, due in October, will decide which of those inquiries happens. Accountability for Oct. 7 has become, by the opposition's design, the campaign's organizing question, and by Tuesday afternoon it had a new document at its center — one whose author's identity is known, whose sources are not, and whose subject says it never happened.

sources.news_title: UAE warned Netanyahu of 7 October attack, Israeli newspaper reports
sources.text:
Israeli Premier Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a political storm and accusations in the middle of Israel’s election campaign that he ignored a direct warning from the UAE about the imminence of Hamas’ 7 October attack in 2023.
UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed allegedly warned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning a major offensive in Israel just days before the militant group launched its attack on 7 October 2023, Israeli daily newspaper Haaretz claimed on Tuesday.
Haaretz reported that at the end of September 2023 — 10 days before the attack — the UAE president spoke with Netanyahu for 45 minutes and said the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation.
The newspaper reported that Bin Zayed told Netanyahu that the attack would lead to bloodshed and could destabilise the region and undermine the Abraham Accords, the normalisation agreements between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority nations.
The Haaretz report claims Netanyahu “reacted with relative calm” and assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario and a possible attack was more likely to come from the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu's office called the report by the left-leaning newspaper "an absolute lie" and denied he spoke to the Emirati leader at that time.
The Haaretz newspaper based its report on a new book, “Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment,” by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval in which they investigate the circumstances and intelligence failures of the 7 October attacks.
Election campaign heating up
The revelations come at a time when Israel’s election campaign is heating up for the vote next month, and Netanyahu’s actions around the time of the 7 October attack are a key issue in the campaign.
Israel’s opposition leaders immediately launched a series of scathing attacks on Netanyahu, culminating in a joint statement calling for an investigation.
“The Israeli public is entitled to know: What did Netanyahu know, when did he know, why he didn’t update the security establishment, and why he didn’t act to protect Israeli civilians?” the joint statement by Naftali Bennett, Gadi Eisenkot, Yair Golan and Avigdor Lieberman said.
“Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch," Bennett, who leads the B’Yachad party, said.
Eisenkot, a former chief of the General Staff of the Israel Defence Forces and a rival to Netanyahu in the upcoming legislative elections, had earlier said the Israeli leader "received dozens of warnings for 7 October and ignored them all."
"He is unfit for office," he added in a post on X.
In a video address, Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, also accused Netanyahu of "endangering Israel" and "leading us to disaster."
"You knew, you ignored, you failed, you are to blame, Netanyahu. The excuses are over," he said.
Netanyahu's office denied the report's veracity on Tuesday evening.
"The press reports are false. No warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October," the office said in a statement, while adding it was possible the two countries exchanged messages through intelligence channels.
The UAE's foreign ministry said on Tuesday it would not comment on the Israeli media report.
In a statement, the ministry said "the UAE government does not comment on media stories or speculation."
"When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."
'Basic strategic failure'
Former Israeli government spokesperson Eylon Levy told Euronews that the 7 October attacks were a "strategic failure" on Israel's part.
"If this report is true, it's hard to say why he wouldn't pass that on, other than that he didn't think it was credible. And that's because Netanyahu was really convinced that Hamas was deterred," Levy said.
"It was a basic strategic failure to understand the nature of the enemy facing Israel, its true intentions and its real capabilities".
Israelis are due to head to the polls on 27 October for a national election to determine the 120-seat Knesset (parliament).
On election day, voters are asked to choose a political party and its list of candidates, rather than choosing individual candidates directly.
Asked about the Haaretz report's impact on Netanyahu's chances in the elections, Levy told Euronews that it was "too early" to rule him out, but that the vote would ultimately be about "responsibility for 7 October."
Netanyahu has so far rejected multiple calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the 7 October attack following other accusations of his handling of the crisis.
During the surprise attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, triggering the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza that ended in a US-brokered peace deal in October 2025.
Israel's offensive resulted in the deaths of more than 73,600 Palestinians in the Strip, according to the Hamas-run Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures do not distinguish civilians and combatants.
The United Nations considers the ministry's figures reliable, and Israeli officials have since stated that the numbers are broadly accurate.
Hundreds of Israelis, mostly soldiers, have been killed in continued fighting in wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

WASHINGTON (TNND) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed's warning about a Hamas attack days before Oct. 7, 2023, and didn't inform his security officials, according to a Tuesday report.
MBZ had a 45-minute phone call with Netanyahu in late September, some 10 days before the attack, warning him that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation against Israel that would result in death, unsettle the region, and potentially harm the Abraham Accords, three senior foreign officials told journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, according to their book, “Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment,” published in the Haaretz newspaper, the Times of Israel reported.
According to the report, MBZ was surprised by Netanyahu’s sanguine response during the call, with the Israeli premier saying that his government was on top of things in Gaza, that any Hamas action would likely occur in the West Bank, and that Israel was prepared for anything.
The Oct. 7 cross-border, multipronged assault by Hamas resulted in 1,200 people killed and 251 hostages taken to Gaza, starting the nearly three-year war.
MBZ became aware of the Hamas threat from Sinwar, who had been frustrated by the lack of progress in negotiations for a Palestinian prisoner release deal with Israel.
Israel reportedly sought to hide its "virtually direct" talks with Hamas in summer 2023, during which the terrorist group initially sought the release of 500 prisoners in exchange for hostages, according to the report.
Sinwar then accepted the release of 50 prisoners, while the Israel Security Agency, known as Shin Bet, was leaning toward accepting the release of 30, with 20 of them serving life sentences, which Netanyahu approved.
The prime minister repeatedly delayed convening the ministerial committee for hostages and missing persons, which needed to approve the prisoner release, an Israeli security source told the journalists. Shin Bet officials managing the talks said that the delay was a result of Netanyahu's fear of leaks to the media.
In early September 2023, amid the breakdown in the talks, Sinwar cut off contact with negotiators. A senior Shin Bet official told Haaretz that Sinwar “vanished from our radar, evaporated.”
Sinwar held two private meetings with a senior Palestinian National Liberation Movement interlocutor referred to as “Coal Eyes,” who was part of the negotiations, in which the terrorist leader told him to warn the Israelis of the consequences if they did not move forward on a deal.
“Tell the Israelis if they don’t advance, I’m preparing a huge surprise for them,” Sinwar was quoted as saying in a conversation with Coal Eyes. “Tell them to expect a zilzal, an earthquake.”
“It was clear to [Coal Eyes] that the operation Sinwar was talking about could affect the entire Middle East, but he was afraid to report the information directly to the Shin Bet. On the other hand, he was even more terrified that if he didn’t update the Shin Bet, the Israelis might accuse him of collaborating with Sinwar. He genuinely feared for his life. Therefore, he decided to convey the message to Bin Zayed,” the journalists wrote.
In Sinwar's second meeting with Coal Eyes, the Hamas leader said he was preparing “a formidable operation.”
Sinwar added that it would be “the mother of all surprises. A terrifying operation. Something extraordinary,” again reportedly using the word zilzal.

JERUSALEM (VINnews) — United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu roughly a week and a half before Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack that the group’s Gaza leader, Yahya Sinwar, was preparing a major operation against Israel, according to a sweeping investigation published Tuesday by Haaretz.

The investigation by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruti Yuval, based on dozens of Israeli and international sources as well as recordings, documents and internal correspondence, alleges that bin Zayed personally contacted Netanyahu in late September 2023 and warned him that Sinwar was preparing a significant move that could lead to widespread bloodshed, destabilize the region and endanger the Abraham Accords.
The report says the conversation lasted approximately 45 minutes and took place between the two leaders directly.
According to Haaretz, bin Zayed told Netanyahu that the intelligence came from a close Palestinian adviser who had moved from Gaza to Abu Dhabi years earlier but maintained extensive contacts inside the Strip. The adviser reportedly told the Emirati leader that Sinwar was preparing what he described as an event of potentially enormous proportions. Bin Zayed urged Netanyahu to take the threat seriously and ensure that Israel was prepared.
The Prime Minister’s Office has categorically rejected the report. In a statement carried by multiple Israeli outlets, Netanyahu’s office said: “An absolute lie! Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him.”
Haaretz, however, stands by its reporting, saying the investigation is based on numerous sources and documentary material. According to the investigation, Netanyahu responded relatively calmly to the Emirati warning. The prime minister reportedly told bin Zayed that, in Israel’s assessment, Hamas’s main focus was on Judea and Samaria rather than Gaza and reassured him that Israel was prepared for any scenario.
The most consequential allegation in the report is that the warning was not subsequently passed on to the heads of Israel’s security establishment.
According to Haaretz, then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, Mossad chief David Barnea and IDF Chief of Staff Herzi Halevi were not aware that Netanyahu had received the alleged warning from the UAE president. Both Bar and Halevi have reportedly said they had no knowledge of such a warning.
The investigation also says bin Zayed subsequently conveyed his concerns to then-CIA Director William Burns, telling him that he believed “something was about to explode.”
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, now chairman of the B’Yachad party, publicly backed the central claim on Tuesday. Bennett said the report that bin Zayed warned Netanyahu about Sinwar’s intentions was true, although he did not publicly explain the source of his information. He also claimed that former Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had warned Netanyahu days before October 7 that Hamas was preparing a major operation.
Bennett accused Netanyahu of bearing “personal and direct responsibility” for the failures that preceded the October 7 attack, arguing that the prime minister should have immediately raised Israel’s level of alert, convened senior military and intelligence officials and gone south to assess the situation.
He called the alleged failure to act on warnings “criminal negligence” and renewed his demand for a state commission of inquiry.
The new report adds another alleged warning to a growing body of accounts concerning intelligence and security assessments in the weeks and days preceding the Hamas assault.
The October 7 failure has already been the subject of extensive investigations into warnings from Israeli intelligence officials, military observers and foreign governments. The question of what Netanyahu personally knew, when he knew it and what action he took has remained one of the most politically contentious issues surrounding the disaster.
The Haaretz investigation also describes other secret contacts in the period immediately before the attack. According to the report, Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani contacted Mossad chief David Barnea around the same period and conveyed that Hamas was prepared to discuss the release of civilian hostages through Qatari mediation. Barnea reportedly responded that Israel was not prepared at that stage to negotiate with Hamas.
The alleged Emirati warning is particularly notable because the UAE had established diplomatic relations with Israel only three years earlier, through the 2020 Abraham Accords. Bin Zayed was therefore not merely a foreign leader receiving intelligence about Hamas, but the leader of a state that had developed a close strategic relationship with Israel.

The prime minister received a warning from the leader of the United Arab Emirates, according to two top Israeli journalists, who are launching a new book on the matter.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned about a large attack from Hamas days before October 7 but his government did not do anything with the information, according to a new report.
Israeli outlet Haaretz cited a book from top journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, who conducted dozens of interviews with sources including senior officials in the country and around the world.
The book, called "Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment," claims that Netanyahu got the warning some 10 days before the attack from Mohammed bin Zayed. He said then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major attack that would lead to a large escalation.
The report went on to say that MBZ was surprised by Netanyahu's response to his warning. He said that his government was on top of developments in Gaza and that potential actions would come from the West Bank. Regardless, Israel was prepared for any scenario, he said.
MBZ said Sinwar was frustrated about the lack of progress in negotiations for a prisoner exchange with Israel, and the threat to conduct what would become the October 7 attacks came from the Hamas leader himself.
Such a deal was on the verge of being completed in the summer of 2023, but Netanyahu repeatedly delayed convening officials who would be involved in approving the decision. One theory was that the doubts could have stemmed from fear of upsetting the hardline faction of his coalition.
By September, Sinwar cut off contact with negotiators in early September 2023, telling a Palestinian negotiator known as "coal eyes" to warn Israel about the consequences of the delays. "Tell them to expect a zilzal, an earthquake," he reportedly said.
"It was clear to him that the operation Sinwar was talking about could affect the entire Middle East, but he was afraid to report the information directly to the Shin Bet. On the other hand, he was even more terrified that if he didn't update the Shin Bet, the Israelis might accuse him of collaborating with Sinwar. He genuinely feared for his life. Therefore, he decided to convey the message to Bin Zayed," the authors wrote.
"Coal eyes" took the warning to MBZ, claiming that zilzal meant war. However, the warning was not conveyed by either party, leading Sinwar to call on him to relay the message that he was preparing "something extraordinary." "Coal eyes" then took the new warning to MBZ, and also to the Shin Bet, the internal security and counterintelligence agency.
Top officials then discussed the warning, but didn't see it as a threat coming from Gaza and failed to act, with one rhetorically asking why Sinwar would send them a warning.
"Either it was because he grew tired of Israel's foot-dragging, wanting to pressure us into an arrangement and not so eager to start a war. Or, as we prefer to think, it was part of his 'Great Deception' plan, and he wanted to test the IDF's readiness," the official added.
MBZ then held a call with Netanyahu, alarmed by the lack of reaction. "He told Netanyahu that Israel should be ready. Concurrently, he recommended trying to find an economic solution for the Strip and calming the West Bank to prevent escalation," the official said.
On October 1, then-Shin Bet head Ronen Bar proposed taking action, including assassinating top officials, but Netanyahu didn't make a decision. Six days later Hamas launched an assault that ended up with 1,200 people killed and the taking of 251 hostages into Gaza, leading to a years-long war that expanded throughout the Middle East.
The Prime Minister's office rejected the report, calling it a "total lie!" "Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and received no warning from him," the office added.

sources.news_title: UAE gave explicit warning to Netanyahu of Hamas plans days before October 7, new book
sources.text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu received an explicit warning about a major operation being planned by Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar shortly before the October 7 attack, according to a new book by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval. The account also alleges that Netanyahu received a separate warning from Egypt in the days before the massacre and later declined to authorize a renewed proposal to target senior Hamas leaders, including Sinwar.
The book, Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, says Sinwar warned that he was preparing a “big surprise” for Israel and twice used the Arabic word zilzal, meaning “earthquake.” The investigation follows an earlier report by Yedioth Ahronoth journalist Smadar Perry, published during the first days of the war, that Egypt had warned Netanyahu of “something unusual, a terrible operation” being prepared by Hamas.
“The story starts earlier,” Eldar said Tuesday, discussing the investigation published by Haaretz. He said the episode began during indirect talks involving Israel, Hamas and Fatah over the return of the bodies of Israeli soldiers Hadar Goldin and Oron Shaul and the release of Hisham al-Sayed and Avera Mengistu, then held in Gaza. When the talks stalled in early September 2023, Eldar said, Sinwar disappeared completely and dropped off the Shin Bet’s radar.
According to Eldar, Sinwar then contacted a Fatah figure and told him: “Pass on to the Israelis that I’m planning a big surprise for them if they don’t make progress.” Sinwar used the word “earthquake,” Eldar said. The Fatah figure, alarmed by the conversation, passed the message to an associate who now serves as an adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Sinwar later repeated the message: “Pass it on to the Israelis, I’m planning an ‘earthquake’ for them.”
The call on a special app
Eldar said then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar received the information on September 15 and passed it to Netanyahu. About a week and a half later, according to the investigation, bin Zayed sought to make sure Netanyahu had received the warning and called him through a special communications system developed by the UAE.
“They have conversations through a unique system. A representative from the embassy arrives with the application, with a phone, and they hold a conversation that lasts 45 minutes,” Eldar said.
During that conversation, the investigation claims, Netanyahu sought to reassure the UAE president, telling him: “We are prepared in Gaza.” Netanyahu reportedly assessed that if trouble erupted, it was more likely to occur in the West Bank. The book says Netanyahu did not subsequently brief then-IDF chief Herzi Halevi, Bar or then-Mossad chief David Barnea about the alleged call.
A similar warning reached the Prime Minister’s Office from then-Egyptian intelligence chief Gen. Abbas Kamel, according to Perry’s earlier report. Kamel reportedly warned Netanyahu of “something unusual, a terrible operation” being prepared by Hamas. Perry said Netanyahu responded: “In Gaza, we are on top of things, we are in control. Our problem is the West Bank, and that is where we are also moving forces.”
“People in the security establishment said, both in the Shin Bet and the IDF, that if we had known about that conversation, we would essentially have received another assessment reinforcing the information that had already arrived on September 15,” Eldar said. He added: “We have documentation. We are fully backed up on this story. We would not have published it without recordings, documentation and cross-checking.”
The investigation also says that on October 1, during a discussion about unrest along the Gaza border and indications that Hamas was seeking to carry out an attack in the West Bank, Bar again recommended targeting senior Hamas leaders, including Sinwar, who he said was “showing signs of arrogance.”
As on previous occasions when such a proposal was raised, Netanyahu replied: “Prepare plans for me and I’ll consider them,” according to the investigation.
“He never said ‘no,’” one senior security official said. “That was always his way of postponing dealing with the problem.” Another official who attended the meeting recalled Netanyahu concluding: “Keep working on the capability, but for now calm the situation.”
According to the investigation, Netanyahu did not mention during the meeting the warnings that had allegedly reached him from the UAE or Egypt.
“If we had known about the warnings, there is a chance it would have given much greater weight to the first message we received from Sinwar,” a senior Shin Bet official said. “Maybe it would also have clarified what was behind his sudden withdrawal from the talks in early September. We might have put one and one together and reached a completely different conclusion, one that could have changed our entire assessment.”
‘A complete lie’; ‘The report is true’
Netanyahu’s office categorically denied the investigation. “A complete lie. Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and received no warning from him,” it said.
Bar and Halevi also said they had not been informed of any warning conveyed by the UAE president.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who recently met bin Zayed, said the report was true. “The report that Netanyahu was warned 10 days before the October 7 massacre about Sinwar’s intentions is true,” Bennett said. He accused Netanyahu of bearing “personal and direct responsibility” for the failure and said his disregard of warnings amounted to “criminal negligence.”
Gadi Eisenkot, former IDF chief of staff and chairman of the Yashar party, said the report added to evidence that Netanyahu had failed to recognize repeated warning signs ahead of October 7.
“More and more signs indicate that Netanyahu led Israel blindly into the October 7 failure,” Eisenkot said. “Netanyahu received dozens of warnings ahead of October 7 and ignored them all. He is unfit.”
The October Council, a group representing families and activists seeking accountability over the October 7 failures, said the focus should extend beyond whether Netanyahu was awakened on the night of the attack.
“Anyone arguing over whether Netanyahu was woken up on the night of October 7 is ignoring the much bigger question: How many times did people try to wake Israel up before the massacre?” the group said.
It called for answers on who received the warnings, what reached the prime minister, what he did with the information and what was or was not passed on to the security establishment.
“Why, despite all the warning signs published since then, did the State of Israel arrive at the morning of October 7 blind and unprepared?” the council said.

There is perhaps no more chilling indictment of modern Christianity than watching pastors, worship leaders, theologians and Christian entertainers spend decades preaching about Jesus Christ, singing His name and building careers upon His church, only to eventually announce that they no longer believe the Bible, no longer believe in God and no longer consider themselves Christians. A huge difference as you’ll soon see.
“And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.” 1 Corinthians 15:45 (KJB)
You can preach Jesus without knowing Him, sing about the cross without trusting it, build a church without being born again and spend an entire lifetime inside Christianity without ever coming to Christ as a guilty sinner in need of a Saviour. The first Adam made us sinners and brought death upon the human race, but the last Adam—the Lord from Heaven—came to save sinners through His shed blood, death, burial and resurrection. If you came to Jesus for healing, happiness, success, acceptance or religious experience, but never came as a lost sinner trusting His finished work, then you came for the wrong reason. On this Sunday Service, we clear away the clutter and present you Jesus, high and lifted up.
The Bible Believers Sunday Service: The Last Adam
The Last Adam, Or The Supremacy of Jesus Christ Over Sin, Death, Religion and the Ruin of Adam
Main Text
“And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit. Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.” 1 Corinthians 15:45–49 (KJB)
Central Truth
Every person is born naturally in Adam, under sin and sentenced to death. The sinner who believes the gospel is spiritually placed in Jesus Christ, receiving righteousness, eternal life and the promise of a glorified body. This is why you must be born again, your first birth is no good.
“Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” John 3:3 (KJB)
The first Adam brought the human race down into death. The last Adam raises believing sinners into everlasting life. Jesus Christ is not one religious option among many—He is God’s final, complete and exclusive answer to everything Adam destroyed.
I. The First Adam Was the Beginning of the Natural Creation
“And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” Genesis 2:7 (KJB)
Adam was created:
- Directly by God.
- In the image of God.
- Without sin.
- With dominion over the earth.
- With the ability and responsibility to obey God.
- As the representative head of the human race.
Adam was not born into the world; he was created by God. Every other naturally conceived human being descends from him and consequently bears his fallen image.
“And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:” Genesis 5:3 (KJB)
Adam was originally created in God’s image, but after the fall he produced children in his own fallen likeness. Humanity inherited more than Adam’s physical characteristics; it inherited his sinful nature and sentence of death.
Application
Our fundamental problem is not our environment, education, economic condition or lack of self-esteem. Our problem is that we are members of Adam’s fallen race.
II. The First Adam Brought Sin and Death Into the World
“Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:” Romans 5:12 (KJB)
Adam’s disobedience brought:
- Sin into the world.
- Death upon mankind.
- Condemnation before God.
- Separation from God.
- Corruption into creation.
- A sinful nature upon Adam’s descendants.
“For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” Romans 5:19 (KJB)
We do not become sinners merely when we commit our first sinful act. We commit sinful acts because we were born with a sinful nature inherited through Adam.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;” Romans 3:23 (KJB)
Application
Education may refine Adam’s descendants. Religion may restrain them. Government may regulate them. Psychology may analyze them. But none of these things can remove a sinner from Adam and place him into Christ.
The sinner does not need renovation—he needs regeneration.
III. Jesus Christ Is the Second Man and the Last Adam
“And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit. Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.” 1 Corinthians 15:45-48 (KJB)
Jesus is called:
- The second man because He is the beginning of a new humanity.
- The last Adam because there will never be another representative head or another divine plan of salvation.
There was a first Adam, but there will never be a third Adam. Jesus Christ is God’s last, complete and eternal answer.
The contrast between the two Adams
| The First Man Adam | The Last Adam Jesus | 
| Came from the earth | Is the Lord from Heaven | 
| Became a living soul | Became a quickening Spirit | 
| Was tested in a garden | Submitted to God in a garden | 
| Disobeyed concerning a tree | Obeyed unto death upon a tree | 
| Brought sin | Bore our sins | 
| Brought condemnation | Provides justification | 
| Brought death | Gives eternal life | 
| Produced a fallen race | Creates one new man | 
| Returned to the dust | Rose bodily from the dead | 
| Bears the earthly image | Gives believers the heavenly image | 
Jesus Christ did not come merely to repair Adam’s old creation. He came to become the Head of an entirely new creation.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJB)
IV. The Supremacy of the Last Adam Is Revealed in His Obedience
Adam was given one prohibition and disobeyed. Jesus Christ faced every temptation and remained completely obedient to His Father.
“For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” Romans 5:19 (KJB)
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” Philippians 2:8 (KJB)
Adam’s disobedience was counted against his race. Christ’s perfect obedience and finished sacrifice are counted for those who believe. We are not saved through our obedience to God. We are saved through faith in what Jesus Christ accomplished through His obedience.
Religion says, ‘Obey so that God may accept you.’
The gospel says, ‘Believe on the One whose obedience has satisfied God completely.’
“Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved.” Ephesians 1:5-7 (KJB)
V. The Last Adam Defeated What the First Adam Released
“For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” 1 Corinthians 15:21–22 (KJB)
Adam brought death, but Christ conquered death through His resurrection.
“Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.” Romans 6:9 (KJB)
Jesus Christ is supreme because:
- His blood satisfies God’s judgment against sin.
- His cross defeated the power of sin.
- His burial demonstrates that He truly died.
- His resurrection conquered death.
- His righteousness justifies the believer.
- His Spirit seals the believer.
- His life guarantees our future resurrection.
Application
Christianity does not rest upon religious feelings, alleged healings, visions, tongues or supernatural experiences. It rests upon the historical death, burial and bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ. If every feeling disappears and every circumstance turns against us, the empty tomb remains empty.
VI. A Sinner Must Change His Position, Not Merely His Behavior
Every person occupies one of two spiritual positions:
- In Adam: condemned, spiritually dead and awaiting judgment.
- In Christ: justified, spiritually alive and possessing eternal life.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” Romans 8:1 (KJB)
A person is not placed into Christ by:
- Being raised in church.
- Attending Bible college.
- Becoming a pastor.
- Building a congregation.
- Preaching sermons.
- Baptizing converts.
- Performing supposed healings.
- Speaking in tongues.
- Feeding the poor.
- Living a respectable life.
“For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.” 1 Corinthians 12:13 (KJB)
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” John 3:16 (KJB)
“Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.” John 3:7 (KJB)
A minister can spend decades talking about Jesus without ever trusting Jesus Christ’s finished work as the payment for his own sins. Religious activity can give a person a reputation, an audience and a career. It cannot give him eternal life.
VII. The Only Saving Message Is the Gospel of Christ
“Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:” 1 Corinthians 15:1–4 (KJB)
A sinner must understand:
- I have sinned against a holy God.
- My sin has earned death and judgment.
- I cannot save myself through religion or good works.
- Jesus Christ died as the payment for my sins.
- He was buried and rose bodily from the dead.
- God will save me when I place my faith in Jesus Christ alone.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJB)
Application
A person may originally enter a church because he is lonely, sick, frightened or searching for answers. But unless he eventually recognizes himself as a guilty sinner and trusts Christ’s finished work, he has not believed the saving gospel.
Jesus did not die merely to improve Adam’s children. He died to save them and place them into Himself.
VIII. When People Come to Jesus for the Wrong Reason
Many people are invited to “come to Jesus” because He supposedly will:
- Heal their bodies.
- Restore their relationships.
- Guarantee success.
- Fulfill their dreams.
- Give them an emotional experience.
- Solve all their earthly problems.
- Make them prosperous and happy.
But those things are not the gospel. Jesus confronted people who followed Him for material benefits rather than because they believed who He was.
“Jesus answered them and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Ye seek me, not because ye saw the miracles, but because ye did eat of the loaves, and were filled.” John 6:26 (KJB)
When the expected healing does not come, the emotional experience fades or life becomes painful, a false convert may conclude that Christianity has failed him. In reality, he may never have trusted the gospel at all. He came for benefits from Jesus without first coming to Jesus as a sinner needing a Saviour.
Teaching Statement
If you came to Jesus only to obtain a better life, but never trusted His shed blood as the payment for your sins, you came for the wrong reason.
IX. Timmy Gibson and the Tragedy of an Empty Pulpit
Timmy Gibson reportedly spent approximately thirty years teaching and preaching, including seventeen years leading a church he founded. He now says he no longer believes the Bible or Christianity and publicly identifies as an atheist. Freedom From Religion Foundation

Gibson’s background emphasized supposed healings, tongues, spiritual experiences and personal transformation. But none of those things proves that a person ever trusted Christ’s death, burial and resurrection as the payment for his sins.
“They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.” Titus 1:16 (KJB)
An important rightly divided distinction
We cannot infallibly see Gibson’s heart or declare from his present atheism alone that he was never saved. Biblically, there are two possible conditions:
- A lost religious professor: He preached about Jesus but never personally trusted the gospel.
- A saved but ruined workman: He once trusted Christ but later abandoned sound doctrine, shipwrecked his testimony and became disqualified for Christian service.
Salvation and service are not identical. A saved man can destroy his ministry, lose his reward and become a castaway without becoming spiritually unborn.
“But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.” 1 Corinthians 9:27 (KJB)
Here “castaway” concerns being rejected or disapproved for service and reward—not losing eternal salvation.
“If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.” 2 Timothy 2:13 (KJB)
Application
Never place your confidence in a preacher’s personality, longevity, church size, education or supernatural claims. Preachers can fall, institutions can collapse and religious experiences can be exposed as counterfeit. Jesus Christ remains exactly who the Bible declares Him to be.
“Let God be true, but every man a liar.” Romans 3:4 (KJB)
X. The Last Adam Must Have the Preeminence
“And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.” Colossians 1:18 (KJB)
Jesus Christ is supreme over:
- Adam and the entire human race.
- Sin and condemnation.
- Satan and spiritual wickedness.
- Religion and human philosophy.
- Every preacher and religious institution.
- Death and the grave.
- Heaven and earth.
- The present creation and the world to come.
A fallen preacher cannot diminish Christ. An atheist cannot dethrone Him. A skeptic cannot disprove Him. A false church cannot replace Him. The last Adam has conquered death and will reign until every enemy is beneath His feet.
“Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:” Philippians 2:9 (KJB)
Closing Challenge
The final question is not:
- Were you raised in church?
- Were you baptized?
- Did you have an emotional experience?
- Did you speak in tongues?
- Did you once answer an altar call?
- Did you become a preacher?
- Did people believe that God was using you?
The question is:
Have you, as a guilty and helpless sinner, placed your faith in the shed blood, death, burial and resurrection of Jesus Christ as the complete payment for your sins? The first Adam cannot save you. Religion cannot save you. A pastor cannot save you. Your experiences cannot save you. Your good works cannot save you. Only the last Adam can take a condemned child of Adam and make him a redeemed, justified and eternally secure member of the body of Christ.
“For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” 1 Corinthians 15:22 (KJB)
The first Adam brought us into the grave. The last Adam came out of the grave—and everyone who trusts Him will come out as well.

Israeli Opposition Demands Netanyahu’s Exit over October 7 Warning
Israeli opposition leaders have intensified calls for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down following a report that the United Arab Emirates warned him of a planned Hamas attack days before the October 7, 2023 assault.
Haaretz reported, citing an excerpt from an upcoming book by two of its journalists, that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan spoke with Netanyahu about a week and a half before the attack and warned that Hamas was preparing a major operation.
Netanyahu’s office has rejected the report as false, insisting that the Israeli prime minister did not speak with the Emirati leader during that period.
The report has nevertheless triggered renewed criticism from Netanyahu’s political opponents, who accuse him of failing to act on warnings about the impending attack and attempting to evade responsibility for the security failures surrounding it.
Former military commander Gadi Eisenkot, regarded as one of Netanyahu’s leading rivals in the October 27 elections, said the prime minister had received multiple warnings before the attack but failed to respond adequately.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett also accused Netanyahu of bearing direct responsibility for the deaths recorded during the October 7 assault and called for his immediate removal from office.
Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats Party, similarly accused Netanyahu of putting Israel’s security at risk and said explanations surrounding the failure to prevent the attack were no longer acceptable.
The controversy has renewed calls for an independent state commission of inquiry into the security and intelligence failures that allowed Hamas to launch the unprecedented assault.
Opposition parties have pledged to establish such a commission as a priority if they win the October 27 elections. The proposed body would have its members appointed by the Supreme Court, but Netanyahu’s government has rejected the proposal.
According to Haaretz, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, who was later killed by Israel, had warned a former Palestinian official that the group was preparing a major operation. The official reportedly passed the information to an Emirati adviser, who then relayed it to the UAE president before the alleged call to Netanyahu.
The UAE established diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020 under the US-brokered Abraham Accords during Donald Trump’s first administration. Netanyahu has frequently presented the relationship with Abu Dhabi as a major diplomatic achievement.
The report also said Netanyahu responded calmly to the alleged warning. It added that his government had for years maintained the status quo with Hamas, including allowing Qatari financial support to reach Gaza, based on the assessment that the group was more focused on preserving itself than pursuing a full-scale war with Israel.
On October 7, 2023, Hamas fighters launched a surprise assault on southern Israel, killing more than 1,200 people and taking about 250 hostages, according to Israeli figures.
Israel responded with a massive military campaign in Gaza that has devastated large parts of the territory and killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, according to the Gaza health ministry, whose figures the United Nations considers broadly reliable.
